subject: AMZN: Utility filings show AWS load commitments up ~1.8GW for 2027-28; our 2027 capex now $188bn vs. Street ~$170bn
body:
CORVANE SECURITIES | Cloud & Internet | Company Note | Oct 13, 2026

AMZN (Buy, PT $285): Power filings point to a step-up in AWS build that is not in numbers

Bottom line: In amended load agreements filed last week in three state utility proceedings (Virginia, Ohio and Mississippi), AWS-affiliated entities increased contracted peak load by about 1.8GW for energy start dates between Q2 2027 and Q4 2028. That is roughly 35% above the load commitments we tracked as of the June filings. We did not see any mention of this in company commentary at the Q2 call, and we have not found it in sell-side models.

What we found:
- The filings are revisions to existing service agreements, which suggests build plans were pulled forward and enlarged rather than being newly announced.
- Two of the three sites include on-site substation upgrades with in-service dates in mid-2027, a signal that the shells are already in construction.
- Our rule of thumb, roughly $35-40bn of all-in capex per GW including servers and networking, implies $60-70bn of incremental spend across 2027-28, with about half of it landing in 2027.

Estimate changes:
- 2027 capex raised to $188bn from $172bn (Street ~$170bn)
- 2027 free cash flow cut to $22bn from $31bn
- 2027 AWS revenue unchanged for now; we think the added capacity supports faster growth in 2028, but we are not yet changing the model for this
- 2027 depreciation up about $2.4bn, roughly 45bp of AWS operating margin

Why it matters: The market is focused on AWS growth (consensus +21% y/y in Q3). The risk is that a higher capex trajectory pressures free cash flow and margin expectations for 2027 before the revenue benefit appears. If management signals higher 2027 capex on the October 29 call, we expect a debate about returns on capital.

What to watch: Q3 capex vs. our $38bn estimate; any change to the "similar to 2026" language on 2027 spending; and whether management links the capacity to specific contracted backlog.

Hannah Lindqvist | Corvane Securities
Full model and filing list attached. Important disclosures at the end of the report.
reason: Uses new utility-filing evidence to argue that AWS data center commitments, and therefore 2027 capex, are materially higher than consensus. The analyst cuts 2027 FCF estimates sharply, and the issue has not been discussed by management or the Street. That is incremental and estimate-changing ahead of the October 29 report.

subject: MedTech: Bariatric procedure volumes soften as GLP-1 scripts climb - 3Q preview and estimate changes
body:
Corrigan Whitlock Securities | Healthcare Equity Research | Industry Update

Bariatric surgery: volumes decelerating faster than we modeled

We update our procedure-volume model ahead of 3Q reporting season (first prints from our coverage start Oct 20).

What our data show:
- Our hospital claims panel (about 640 U.S. facilities) shows sleeve gastrectomy and gastric bypass volumes down 9.4% y/y in August, versus -6.1% in 1H26.
- Weekly GLP-1 prescriptions for obesity are up roughly 38% y/y, with the sharpest growth in the 35-45 BMI cohort that historically fed the surgical funnel.
- Consult-to-surgery conversion at the 40 largest centers fell to 41% from 47% a year ago. Surgeons say patients increasingly try drug therapy for 6-9 months before booking.
- Offsetting: revision procedures (patients regaining weight after drug discontinuation) are +14% y/y, though from a small base.

Estimate changes:
- Stapler and energy-device vendors: we trim 3Q bariatric revenue by 3-5% and 4Q by 5-7%. Bariatric is under 4% of sales for the large diversified names, so total company EPS impact is 1-2 cents.
- Specialty bariatric players (pure-play surgical devices): we cut 2027 revenue growth to flat from +4%.

Stock views: No rating changes. We prefer orthopedics and cardiac ablation names, where we see volume tailwinds from an aging cohort and where GLP-1 exposure is minimal. Our two bariatric-heavy small caps move to Neutral on valuation after a 22% run since July.

Risks: Faster oral GLP-1 adoption, a payer shift to cover surgery earlier in the care pathway, or supply normalization that lowers drug prices.

Full model and claims-panel methodology attached.

Hannah Voss, PhD | Corrigan Whitlock Securities
Important disclosures appear at the end of the attached report.

subject: RECAP: Alphabet ad tech remedies hearing - judge presses both sides on divestiture timeline
body:
CAPITOL SIGNAL | TECH POLICY ALERT | Oct 13

Recap of last Thursday's public remedies hearing in the DOJ ad tech case (Alphabet/Google)

For readers catching up, here is what was said in open court on Oct 8:

- DOJ reiterated its request for divestiture of the AdX exchange and a phased open-sourcing of auction logic. This is the same remedy sought in its filings since the spring.
- Google's counsel again argued that behavioral remedies (interoperability commitments, no first/last look, data-use limits) would resolve the court's concerns without a breakup, and said a divestiture would take 18-24 months to execute.
- The judge questioned both sides on how a divestiture would be monitored, and asked DOJ whether a trustee model had been used in comparable matters. She gave no indication of her leaning.
- The court said it expects to rule by year-end. That is consistent with the schedule published in August.
- Google confirmed that it will appeal any adverse ruling.

Context: Ad networks revenue is roughly 10% of Alphabet's total revenue, per the company's latest filing. Sell-side coverage this week has largely treated the hearing as no change to the base case, and most brokers continue to model no revenue impact from remedies in 2027.

No ruling was issued. We will alert you if the court posts an order.

Dalton Reyes | Capitol Signal News

subject: Quick note - seeing odd Google ad auction behavior across our retail accounts
body:
Marcus,

Good catching up at the breakfast last month. Wanted to pass along something we're seeing, with the caveat that it's anecdotal and I can't tell yet if it means anything.

We run paid search for roughly 60 mid-to-large retail and consumer brands. Over the last two and a half weeks, across about a dozen of our biggest accounts, we've seen cost-per-click on non-brand shopping campaigns drift up about 9-12% vs. the same period last year, while impression share on those campaigns has been flat to slightly down. That's a faster pace of inflation than we saw in Q3, when CPCs were up closer to mid-single digits y/y.

Two possible explanations:
1. Holiday budgets being front-loaded earlier than usual, since several clients pulled their Q4 planning forward by a couple of weeks.
2. Changes on Google's side. A few of our reps mentioned (informally) that the AI-generated results placement has been shifting around, and our click-through rates on some product listing ads are down even as spend is up.

What we don't know: whether this is a broad pattern or just our client mix. Our book skews toward apparel, home goods and sporting goods, so it may not generalize to travel, financial services or auto. We also have not yet checked whether conversion rates held, which would change the read entirely. We should have a cleaner view by the end of next week once the October data settles.

Happy to share the account-level charts (anonymized) if useful. Please don't forward outside your team.

Best,
Tom

Brightwell Digital Partners

CORVANE CAPITAL MARKETS | TECHNOLOGY MORNING BRIEF | Oct 13, 2026

Theme: Hyperscaler capex heading into the earnings window

With the large cloud providers set to report over the next two weeks, we revisit the capex picture. Nothing here is new, but it frames what we expect to hear.

Where we are:
- Combined capex for the top-four U.S. cloud providers is tracking to a ~$400bn annualized run-rate based on trailing two-quarter disclosures.
- Management teams have consistently signaled that 2027 spend will grow again, with data center construction, networking and custom silicon taking a rising share.
- Roughly 55-60% of spend is on servers and accelerators (short-lived assets) with the balance in land, buildings and power.

What the Street already expects:
- Consensus assumes 2027 capex growth in the mid-teens, in line with the commentary on prior calls.
- Depreciation growth is the main margin debate, and every sell-side shop has flagged that useful-life assumptions will pressure operating margin by 100-150bp in 2027.
- Power availability, not chip supply, is described as the binding constraint for most operators.

Our view: We continue to expect the group to guide capex higher, to be rewarded where AI revenue growth keeps pace, and to be penalized where cloud growth decelerates against a rising spend base. This is consistent with our September note and with the consensus narrative.

No changes to ratings or estimates across coverage.

BELLWETHER WIRE | SEMICONDUCTORS | Oct 13, 9:42am ET

Nvidia's FQ3 setup: what the Street already expects

With Nvidia due to report in November, a review of published sell-side models shows a tight consensus on the main drivers:

- Data center revenue: consensus sits near 88% of total revenue, with sequential growth in the high-single digits to low-double digits. Estimates have drifted up roughly 2% over the past 30 days.
- Blackwell mix: Most models assume Blackwell-family products exceed 70% of data center compute revenue, up from roughly 60% last quarter, with the remainder largely Hopper-based and networking.
- Gross margin: The Street expects non-GAAP gross margin in the mid-70s, consistent with management's prior commentary of stabilizing as the ramp matures.
- Customer concentration: Analysts continue to flag that a handful of hyperscalers account for roughly half of data center sales, and tie Nvidia's growth rate to cloud capex guidance from Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon and Meta in the coming weeks.
- Risks cited repeatedly: export-license uncertainty for China-bound products, power and cooling constraints at customer sites, and competition from custom accelerators.

Our read: The debate is less about the quarter and more about 2027 durability, which analysts widely link to the pace of hyperscaler capex commitments. Nothing in the published numbers points to a major surprise in either direction.

Options market implies a roughly 7% move on the print, in line with the trailing four-quarter average.

This item is a summary of publicly available estimates and is not investment advice.

Bellwether Wire | Newsroom

subject: Muni Update: Federal court order on state pension disclosure rules - what it means for issuers
body:
Dunmore Hale Securities | Public Finance Strategy | Special Update

Court vacates state pension disclosure rule: implications for muni issuers

On Monday, a federal appeals court vacated a rule requiring state and local governments to publish standardized pension-funding assumptions within 120 days of fiscal year-end. The panel held that the issuing agency exceeded its statutory authority in setting uniform actuarial inputs.

Key points:
- The ruling applies to roughly 1,900 issuers that had been preparing for the January 2027 compliance date.
- The agency may appeal en banc or restart rulemaking, but we think a new proposal is unlikely before mid-2027.
- Disclosures will revert to existing accounting standards, which allow wide variation in discount-rate assumptions (we see a range of 5.8% to 7.4% across large state plans).

Market impact: We expect modest widening of 3-6bp for weaker-funded issuers (Illinois, New Jersey, Kentucky) as investors price in less comparability. Higher-rated issuers should be little affected. Primary supply is unchanged at roughly $42bn for October.

What we are doing: We maintain our overweight to essential-service revenue bonds and a modest underweight to general-obligation debt from the weakest-funded states.

This court decision has no bearing on corporate disclosure rules.

Alan Pritchett | Dunmore Hale Securities
For institutional clients only.

CALLOWAY HARTWELL RESEARCH | Semiconductors | Oct 13, 2026

NVDA (Buy, PT unchanged): Recapping the themes into the November print

With the group quiet ahead of earnings, we summarize what has been widely reported over the past several weeks and where we stand.

1. Blackwell Ultra ramp. Multiple outlets and supply-chain sources have reported that Blackwell Ultra rack shipments are ramping through the October quarter, with TSMC advanced packaging capacity the main gating factor. 2. China. Press reports continue to describe uncertainty around export licensing for data center products to China. Management has already guided to no China data center revenue in its outlook, so we treat any approval as upside and not as a base case.

3. Hyperscaler capex. The large cloud providers have all raised 2026 capex plans in the past year, and 2027 commentary has been constructive. Our model assumes top-four capex growth of roughly 30% in 2027, in line with Street.

4. Networking. Networking revenue growth has outpaced compute in recent quarters, as the company has said publicly.

Estimates and valuation:
- FQ3 revenue: $76.4bn (consensus $76.0bn)
- FQ3 non-GAAP gross margin: 74.5% (guide: ~74-75%)
- We keep our Buy rating and PT based on 28x CY27 EPS.

subject: BREAKING: Fifth Circuit vacates agency overdraft-fee rule; nationwide effect, bank trade groups win
body:
COURTLINE LEGAL ALERTS | Federal Appeals | Oct 13, 2026 | 10:42am ET

FIFTH CIRCUIT VACATES FEDERAL OVERDRAFT-FEE RULE IN 2-1 DECISION

A divided three-judge panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit today vacated the consumer financial regulator's rule capping overdraft fees at large depository institutions. The court held that the agency exceeded its statutory authority by treating overdraft charges as credit under the Truth in Lending framework.

KEY POINTS
- Scope: Vacatur applies nationwide, not only to the plaintiff trade associations' members.
- Reasoning: The majority found that Congress did not clearly authorize the agency to set a price ceiling for overdraft services, citing the major questions doctrine.
- Dissent: Judge Ainsley Prewitt argued that the agency's reading was reasonable given the statute's definition of finance charges and that the case should have been remanded rather than vacated.
- Effective date: The rule was set to take effect January 1, 2027, and covered institutions with more than $10bn in assets.
- Next steps: The agency has 45 days to seek rehearing en banc, and a petition for certiorari is possible. A spokesperson said it is "reviewing the decision."

MARKET CONTEXT
Regional bank shares were modestly higher in early trading. Industry estimates have put annual overdraft revenue at roughly $8bn across affected institutions, and several banks had already trimmed fees ahead of the rule.

Related filings: Docket No. 26-10418 (5th Cir.). Opinion text available to subscribers.

Courtline Legal Alerts is a news service and does not provide legal advice. Manage alert topics in your account settings.

CORVANE INDUSTRIAL GASES (CVN) - INITIATE AT OVERWEIGHT, $214 TARGET

Thesis: Roughly 61% of Corvane's operating profit comes from on-site supply contracts. These are 15-20 year take-or-pay agreements to customers in semiconductors, steel and chemicals. The market treats Corvane as a cyclical gas distributor at 13x EV/EBITDA, but we think the on-site business deserves a multiple closer to a regulated utility.

Evidence:
- Contract structure: 87% of on-site revenue is take-or-pay, with an average remaining term of 11.4 years. Energy costs are passed through with a 30-60 day lag.

- Backlog: $6.3bn of projects under construction, 72% starting up in 2027-28, which supports 6-7% EBITDA growth even with flat industrial production.

Valuation: Our SOTP implies $214/share (+28%). Sensitivity: each 1-turn change in the on-site multiple moves our target by about $11.

Risks: Customer concentration (top 10 are 34% of on-site revenue), a delayed hydrogen build-out, and European power costs.

Marlowe Parcel Analytics | Client Pulse | Oct 13, 2026

Summary

Our monthly panel of 31 regional last-mile and linehaul carriers showed a notable pattern in September. A mid-sized Midwest freight consolidator that reports to our panel (we'll call it Carrier M) recorded inbound pallet volumes tied to third-party seller consignments destined for Amazon fulfillment centers up ~23% y/y, vs. +9% in August and +7% in Q2.

Supporting data points:
- Carrier M: ~1,900 pallets/week in Sept vs. ~1,540 a year ago; the company attributes this to "early holiday inventory builds and sellers pre-positioning ahead of fee changes."
- Two other panel carriers in the Southeast and Mountain West showed +11% and +6% on similar lanes; the rest of the panel was flat to slightly negative.
- Average dwell time at three FBA-type facilities increased by ~0.6 days (Carrier M), which could indicate congestion or early peak stocking.

Caveats: This is one carrier with outsized movement; the other two are within normal range. We cannot rule out customer-specific effects (Carrier M signed a large seller aggregator in July). Panel has a limited share of national volume (~2-3% est.).

Potential read-through: If sellers are pulling inventory forward into Amazon's network, it may reflect expectations of stronger holiday demand or concerns about Q4 storage fee schedules. It could also mean seller-owned inventory is piling up. We would watch October data and Amazon's commentary on inventory placement and fulfillment costs on Oct 29.

Regional carrier results by lane attached (Excel). Contact us to discuss methodology.

Best,
Priyanka Desai
Marlowe Parcel Analytics

sender: Tomas Reidel, Senior Analyst, Pinecrest Channel Research
subject: GOOGL: Colo and neocloud checks suggest Google is placing TPU capacity in third-party sites for outside customers - not in Street numbers
body:
Raj / Ellen,

Short channel-check note ahead of the Oct 27 print. We spoke with seven contacts over the past ten days: three colocation/data center operators (TX, NV, OH), two neocloud operations leads, one electrical contractor on a build-out, and a former Google hardware deployment manager (left spring 2026).

What we heard:

1. Two of the three colo operators and one neocloud contact independently described Google-managed TPU pods being installed, or contracted for installation, in third-party facilities. They said Google owns and operates the hardware and the host provides only power, space and cooling. Delivery timing was described as "Q1 2027 onward."

2. Aggregate scale across the three sites is roughly 150-250MW of critical IT load. One operator said the contract has a take-or-pay structure with a 5-year term.

3. The former Google contact said the purpose is to serve external customers who want TPU capacity inside their own preferred regions or near existing GPU clusters, rather than to relieve Google's internal capacity. She called it "a different motion from Cloud TPU as sold today."

4. The contractor said a fourth site, with higher-density liquid-cooling specs, is in permitting. He did not know the end customer.

Why it matters: We could not find this in any sell-side note, in management commentary, or in the capex-guide discussion we have read. If 200MW is representative and Google earns $9-11m of annual revenue per MW at blended pricing, that is roughly $1.8-2.2bn of annualized run-rate, or about 2% of 2027 Cloud revenue consensus (~$98bn). The bigger effect may be strategic. It would show TPUs becoming a merchant-style product, which changes the competitive framing against GPU-based clouds and could raise capex beyond the ~$185bn Street 2027 figure if the hardware sits on Google's balance sheet.

Caveats: These are anecdotal checks, and three of the seven sources overlap in geography. We have not confirmed customer names. Pricing and margin are our estimates. Mixed sourcing quality, but the specifics (take-or-pay, Google-owned hardware, host-provided power only) were consistent across contacts who do not know each other.

What to watch on the call: any language on "TPU availability in customer-chosen environments," a change in capex phasing commentary, and backlog growth vs. the prior quarter.

Happy to connect you with the contractor and the operator by phone, with the usual compliance screen.

Tomas Reidel
Pinecrest Channel Research

sender: Daniel Okafor, Founder, Brightwater Search Partners (channel checks)
subject: Google Search: 3 of 5 agency heads say AI Overviews ad load is pulling commercial-query clicks down 9-12% since Sept 22
body:
Raj, Marcus,

Following up on the paid search checks we run each quarter. We spoke to five heads of search at mid-to-large performance agencies (combined ~$1.9bn in annual Google spend, mix of retail, travel, financial services and consumer electronics) between Oct 6 and Oct 12.

What is new this quarter:

1. Three of five independently said that since roughly Sept 22 their commercial-intent queries ("best X", "X vs Y", "buy X near me") are showing an expanded AI answer unit above the ads on a much larger share of searches than in August. All three reported paid click volume on those query groups down 9-12% vs. the prior four weeks at flat bids. The other two saw no change.

2. Offsetting this, CPCs on the affected groups are up 6-8% as advertisers bid more for the remaining slots. Net spend is roughly flat, but impressions and conversions are down. One agency head said: "We are paying more for fewer clicks and the client's CFO is asking why."

3. Two agencies said they have moved 5-8% of budget on those groups to Performance Max and shopping placements, where volume looks stable. One has trialed a competing retail media network for the first time.

4. None of them has been told about this by their Google reps. One rep reportedly described it as "a test in a limited set of markets." Two of the agencies are U.S.-heavy, so the footprint does not look limited.

Our take: This is a small sample and we cannot rule out seasonality or a single account mix effect. But the pattern (volume down, price up, advertisers shifting formats) is the first time we have heard click compression on commercial queries described this concretely. Our September-quarter checks last month showed no such effect, and Street models we have seen assume stable paid click growth of low-to-mid single digits for Q4.

We will re-poll another eight agencies by Friday. Full notes from all five calls attached.

Daniel Okafor
Brightwater Search Partners
reason: New, specific channel-check evidence that expanded AI answer units may be cutting paid clicks on commercial queries 9-12% at flat bids, which is not in Street models of stable click growth. sender: Katherine Brandt, Senior Analyst, Elmstead Capital Markets
subject: AMZN: Kuiper-to-Prime Video ad bundle and a sharp cut in 3P fulfillment fees to meet a rival's undercut - est. changes, PT to $265
body:
Elmstead Capital Markets | Internet & Digital Commerce | Company Update

AMZN (Buy) | PT $265 (from $248) | Price: $221

Summary: Our field work this month has uncovered a pricing change that we think is not in numbers. Amazon is quietly rolling out a tiered reduction in FBA fulfillment fees for sellers that also commit to Amazon's Sponsored Products and DSP minimums. We think this is a response to a low-cost logistics rival that has been winning seller share in home and apparel, and it reflects a more aggressive stance on seller retention than we modeled.

What we found:
- Eleven of 14 sellers we surveyed (avg. $18m GMV) received notices dated Oct 1-8 showing FBA fee cuts of 7-12% effective Nov 1, conditional on a 15% minimum ad spend commitment tied to GMV.
- Sellers expect to be net winners on total cost by 3-4 points of GMV, but only if they hit ad commitments.
- Two large aggregators told us the logistics rival had offered rates up to 18% below FBA on bulky items in September.

Our model changes:
- Fulfillment revenue growth trimmed by about 60bp in Q4 and 2027 (lower rates, partly offset by volume gains).
- Advertising revenue raised: we now assume 2027 ad growth of 18.5% (from 17.0%) given the commitment structure. Net impact: 2027 operating income +$1.4bn, FY27 EPS +$0.12 to $7.18.
- Q3 est. unchanged; Q4 EBIT raised by $0.3bn on ad timing.

Why it matters: Consensus assumes fulfillment fees are a stable source of unit margin and that ads grow about 17%. This move trades a small amount of fulfillment margin for a firmer lock on seller ad spend. It also signals that third-party logistics is now competitive enough to force pricing action, which we think the market has not considered.

Risks: Seller pushback on forced ad minimums; FTC scrutiny of bundled commitments; execution complexity in the holiday period.

Katherine Brandt, Elmstead Capital Markets. Important disclosures are on page 6.

ATLAS INSIGHT CALLS | Transcript Summary | Call date: Oct 12, 2026

Expert: Former Senior Assistant Attorney General, Antitrust Bureau at a large state AG office (left March 2026). 9 years in role, including two multistate retail-platform inquiries.
Interviewer: Atlas client (buy-side)

Key takeaways (summary prepared by Atlas; full transcript attached):

1. Where the process stands. The expert said a coalition of several state AG offices has been reviewing Amazon's marketplace pricing and fair-pricing enforcement practices, separate from the federal case, since early this year. They described the matter as "past the document-request stage and into term-sheet conversations," but stressed that they have no first-hand knowledge of the current state of play and are relying on former colleagues.

2. What a resolution could look like. The expert's base case is a consent decree rather than litigation: Amazon would stop penalizing sellers (via Buy Box suppression or search demotion) for lower prices on rival sites, and would accept an independent monitor for roughly three years. They did not expect a monetary penalty above "low hundreds of millions."

3. Timing. "Realistically, this could be announced anywhere between six weeks and nine months from now." The expert said coalitions like this often wait for a quiet news window, and that a settlement announced around earnings is possible but not something they would bet on.

4. Economic effect. The expert said the commercial impact would mostly depend on how the order interacts with Amazon's seller fee structure. They pointed out that Amazon already changed its fair-pricing language twice in the past two years, and that a formal order might add little beyond what is in place. They were not able to size any effect on third-party seller services revenue.

5. Interviewer note: The expert was candid that their view reflects secondhand conversations. They declined to name individuals or offices still involved.

Compliance: Expert affirmed no MNPI and no confidentiality obligations breached. They did not share information obtained from privileged sources.

Full transcript (11 pages) attached. Reply to schedule a follow-up with this expert or to request a second former-staff perspective.

subject: Calloway Compounders - October issue: Brannock Fastener Supply and the economics of the unglamorous reorder
body:
CALLOWAY COMPOUNDERS LETTER | October 2026 | Featured company deep dive

Brannock Fastener Supply (BFS): why a boring distributor earns a 22% return on capital

Brannock is a $3.4bn market cap distributor of fasteners, seals and small hardware to manufacturers, with roughly 190,000 SKUs and 41,000 active customers. Revenue was $2.1bn over the last twelve months. We think the business is better than its reputation, and this issue explains why.

1) The reorder engine. About 63% of sales come from customers who have ordered in each of the last eight quarters. Brannock places inventory bins and vending cabinets on customer floors, which raises switching costs. Cabinet-served accounts grew spend by 9% last year versus 3% for non-cabinet accounts.

2) Pricing power in small tickets. Median order value is $410. For a customer, the cost of a stockout on a $4 part is a stopped line, so price sensitivity is low. Brannock has passed through roughly 95% of input cost inflation since 2021 with a gross margin that has held between 49.5% and 51.0%.

3) Capital efficiency. Capex is under 1.5% of sales, working capital turns 4.1x and ROIC reached 22% last year. Management has repurchased 6% of shares over three years while keeping net debt at 1.3x EBITDA.

4) What could go wrong. Industrial production is flat, and 28% of sales are tied to heavy equipment and ag machinery, both soft. A large online competitor has been testing next-day delivery in two regions. Our channel work suggests share loss so far is below 1 point.

Valuation: At $64, the stock trades at 17x our 2027 EPS of $3.75, roughly in line with its five-year average. We see a base-case total return of 11-13% annually, with upside if cabinet penetration reaches the 35% management has targeted (currently 27%).

Full model and customer survey data are available to subscribers. Next issue: a regional title insurer.

subject: Invitation: Brookmere Macro Roundtable - Brazil's fiscal framework and the real, Thu Oct 22, 11:00am ET (webinar)
body:
Dear Ellen,

Brookmere Global Strategy invites you to our October Macro Roundtable, a 45-minute client webinar with Q&A.

Topic: Brazil's fiscal framework after the budget revision - what it means for the real, local rates and sovereign spreads

Date: Thursday, October 22, 11:00am-11:45am ET
Speakers:
- Dr. Mariana Teixeira, Head of Latin America Strategy, Brookmere
- Colin Rhodes, Senior EM Rates Strategist, Brookmere
- Moderator: Dominic Hartwell

What we will cover:

1. The budget revision. The government's revised 2027 budget assumes a primary surplus target of 0.25% of GDP, with a tolerance band of 0.25 points either side. Our estimate is that meeting even the lower bound requires roughly 0.9% of GDP in new revenue measures, much of which still needs congressional approval.

2. Central bank path. With the policy rate at 13.25% and inflation expectations drifting to 4.6% for 2027, we see room for only 75bp of cuts through mid-2027, versus about 150bp priced in the swaps curve.

body:
Brackenridge Capital Markets | Internet | Company Update

GOOGL (Outperform): EU non-compliance decision goes beyond provisional findings. Estimates down modestly; thesis intact but Street is not modeling the structure.

What happened
The European Commission adopted its final non-compliance decision on search self-preferencing under the Digital Markets Act yesterday. Three elements matter for numbers:
1. Fine of EUR 2.9bn (about $3.4bn), non-deductible. We expect it booked in 4Q26.
2. Google must remove or fundamentally redesign vertical search units (shopping, hotels, flights, local) in EEA results. The compliance deadline is 90 days, so around Jan 10.
3. Rival vertical providers must be given parity in ranking and data access on non-discriminatory terms. This is a materially broader remedy than the provisional findings, which pointed to "choice-screen-style" tweaks.

Our estimate changes
We estimate EEA Search at about $41bn in 2027E (roughly 17% of Search). Shopping and vertical units drive about 25% of that, or about $10.3bn. We assume a 17% revenue loss on those surfaces before mitigation, partly offset by higher text-ad auction density, for a net 2027E Search hit of $1.6bn.

- 2027E Search revenue: -$1.6bn to $243.4bn (-0.7%); about 1.2% below consensus
- 2027E total revenue: -0.3% to $487.6bn
- 2027E operating income: -$1.2bn, as flow-through is high and compliance spend adds about $150m
- 2027E EPS: $13.30 to $13.22 (-$0.08)
- 4Q26E: only about $0.2bn revenue impact (implementation in January). The one-time fine would hit GAAP EPS by about $0.28; we exclude it from our non-GAAP view.
- 2028E EPS: -$0.10 as the full-year effect lands

Why it matters beyond the model
- Consensus appears to assume a fine plus design tweaks. We think the vertical-unit removal is the part not in numbers, and we expect other regulators (UK, Japan) to look at the template.
- Mitigation is credible: Google has historically recouped a large share of lost shopping revenue through auction changes. We assume 35% recovery in 2027 and 50% in 2028. Upside risk if the recovery is faster.
- An appeal is likely and could delay the redesign. We do not model it.

Valuation: PT to $295 from $300 (22x 2027E EPS ex-cash). We remain Outperform on AI-driven Search resilience and Cloud margin expansion, but expect a modest negative revision cycle ahead of the Oct 27 print.

Gareth Lindqvist | Brackenridge Capital Markets

sender: Imogen Farrow, Founder, Kessling Field Research
subject: Channel check: iOS 27 beta users + app developers flag Siri queries routing to Gemini-based model - small sample, needs confirming
body:
Ellen, Raj, Marcus,

A short unsolicited read from our developer panel. Treat this as anecdotal; we have not been able to validate it independently.

What we heard
We spoke with 9 independent iOS developers and 3 mobile agency leads between Oct 6 and Oct 12, all running the iOS 27 developer beta. Seven of the nine said that when they test the new Siri "complex request" flow, the system prompt that appears the first time asks users to approve processing by a "partner model", and the network traces they captured show calls going to Google-owned endpoints. Two shared packet captures with us (we have not independently verified them). The other two said they had not seen the prompt on their devices.

Details the group volunteered
- Query volume: one agency lead estimated 25-30% of their test Siri sessions are being handed off rather than handled on-device, higher than the 10-15% they expected from Apple's WWDC messaging.
- Latency: handoff responses averaged 1.8-2.4 seconds in their testing.
- Billing question: two developers said an Apple contact told them there would be "no per-call charges to developers," which makes them wonder how the traffic is being paid for, and whether it runs through a Google Cloud arrangement.

Why it might matter, and why we are cautious
If the handoff share is genuinely this high, it would point to more Google cloud/model usage tied to the iPhone installed base than we think is modeled, and to a possible AI cost line for Apple. But the sample is small, beta behavior often changes before launch, and test traffic is not representative of consumer usage. We could not get anyone at either company to comment.

Next steps: We are recruiting 15-20 more beta users and will rerun on the next beta build, expected around Oct 20. Happy to share the two captures if useful.

Best,
Imogen Farrow
Kessling Field Research

HALYARD EXPERT NETWORK | Transcript Summary | Call date: Oct 9, 2026

Expert: Former case team member at the European Commission's competition directorate (left 2025). Worked on information requests in digital and semiconductor markets for six years.
Interviewer: Halyard client (buy-side, TMT)

Key takeaways (summary prepared by Halyard; full transcript attached):

1. Where the process stands. The expert said that, based on conversations with former colleagues, the Commission has moved from informal market questionnaires to a more structured set of information requests to customers and distributors of AI accelerators, including questions on bundling of GPUs with networking and software, and on allocation priority during supply shortages. The expert said he could not confirm whether a formal investigation will be opened.

2. Timing. A formal opening decision, if it came, would likely not occur before the first quarter of 2027. He described the current stage as "fact gathering that can still fizzle." Historically about a third of such preliminary inquiries are closed without formal proceedings.

3. What would matter for Nvidia. The expert believes the allocation-priority question is the most sensitive, as complaints reportedly came from smaller cloud providers. Remedies, if any, would more likely be behavioral (transparency on allocation, unbundling of software) than structural, and would take at least 18-24 months.

4. Financial exposure. Fines under EU rules can reach 10% of global revenue, but he said that outcome is "very unlikely" for a first case of this type. The more likely issue is commercial: customers using the inquiry as leverage in pricing talks.

5. Interviewer note: The expert was clear that his information was secondhand and several months old in places.

Compliance: Expert affirmed no MNPI and no confidentiality obligations breached.

Full transcript (11 pages) attached. Reply to schedule a follow-up.

FENNIMORE HART PARTNERS | Channel Research | Oct 13

CLOUD CHANNEL CHECK: Tone shifting on committed-spend deals

We spoke with nine cloud resellers and managed service partners over the past two weeks (five primarily Google Cloud partners, four primarily AWS partners; all U.S. based, mid-market to large enterprise). This is a small sample and anecdotal.

1. Google Cloud: Four of five partners said their account teams have become noticeably more flexible on multi-year commits in recent weeks. 4. What we can't say: Whether any of this is an end-of-quarter push that will fade after September books close, or a lasting pricing shift. Two partners suggested it was timing-related. None quantified a revenue impact.

Takeaway: Both vendors may be defending share in large enterprise deals ahead of earnings (GOOGL Oct 27, AMZN Oct 29). We would watch cloud backlog commentary and any change in operating margin guidance for signs that concessions are material. No change to our estimates at this time.

Colleen Abara | Fennimore Hart Partners

subject: Federal notice: Pipeline safety agency proposes revised leak-detection reporting thresholds - what the comment period means
body:
Tidewell Securities | Energy & Regulatory Strategy | Policy Note

PHMSA-style proposed rule on leak-detection reporting: what's in it

A federal pipeline safety agency published a notice of proposed rulemaking in the Federal Register last week that would revise leak-detection and reporting requirements for interstate natural gas transmission lines. Comments are due Dec 14.

Key proposals:
- Operators would need to report any leak over 25 barrels equivalent within 6 hours (currently 24 hours)
- Continuous monitoring requirements would expand to lines within a half mile of high-consequence areas
- Operators would have 36 months to install advanced detection on affected segments
- The agency estimates compliance costs of $1.4bn over ten years, concentrated in older Appalachian and Gulf Coast systems

Our read:
We think the final rule is unlikely before late 2027 and that industry will win some flexibility on the monitoring timeline. We estimate the median large midstream operator would see a capex impact of 1-2% of annual spend. Sensor and software vendors with pipeline exposure are the clearest beneficiaries.

What to watch: Industry comments (likely mid-November), any congressional pushback, and whether the agency softens the 6-hour reporting window.

This note is for informational purposes and does not change ratings in our midstream coverage.

Miriam Szekely | Tidewell Securities
Disclosures available on request.

sender: Marguerite Aubry, Senior Airlines Analyst, Castlegate Securities
subject: Airlines: DOT final rule on ancillary-fee disclosure and refund timelines - what it means for 2027 margins
body:
Castlegate Securities | Airlines & Aerospace | Regulatory Update

DOT issues final rule on fee disclosure and automatic refunds

The Department of Transportation yesterday published a final rule in the Federal Register requiring U.S. and foreign carriers to (1) show baggage, change and cancellation fees alongside the base fare in all search results, and (2) issue automatic refunds within 7 business days for card purchases when a flight is cancelled or significantly changed. The rule is effective in 120 days, with a 12-month phase-in for the fee-display requirement on third-party channels.

Why this looks bigger than it is:
- The refund requirement mostly codifies practices that the large carriers adopted voluntarily after the 2022 enforcement actions. We estimate 85% of cancellation-related refunds are already issued within the new window.
- Fee display affects mainly the ultra-low-cost carriers, where ancillary revenue is 40-50% of total revenue. We estimate a 40-60bp hit to 2027 revenue at the ultra-low-cost carriers from lower attach rates, and 10-15bp for the network carriers.
- Litigation is likely. Two airline trade groups have signaled a petition for review in the D.C. Circuit, although a stay before the effective date seems unlikely.

Estimates: We trim 2027E EPS for our two ultra-low-cost names by 1-2% and leave the network carriers unchanged. Ratings and price targets are unchanged.

Other items:
- September traffic: Domestic load factors were 85.6%, down 70bp y/y; unit revenue is trending +1-2% for the quarter.
- Jet fuel: Gulf Coast jet fuel averaged $2.31/gal in September, -4% m/m.

Marguerite Aubry | Castlegate Securities
Important disclosures appear at the end of this report.

WHITMORE LANE | Electrical Equipment & Infrastructure | Read-Through Note

Harlan-Voss Construction (HVC) pre-announced September-quarter results after the close yesterday and held a short call with sell-side analysts. Backlog and revenue were fine. What matters for the megacap complex is what management said about timing.

Key comments from HVC (our paraphrase; no transcript yet):
- Hyperscale data center backlog rose 6% q/q to $14.1bn, but roughly $1.9bn of 2027 project starts were "re-phased" by owners, mostly pushed one to two quarters.

- Management said no customer cancelled projects, and described demand as "intact, with lumpier timing."
- Two of its five largest hyperscale customers asked for revised schedules; it did not name them.

One contractor's re-phasing cannot tell us about total spend, and HVC's data center book is only a small slice of national activity. It does, however, fit with the supply-side tightness we have been seeing in electrical gear, and it is the first contractor datapoint that explicitly links owner design changes to schedule shifts.

- MSFT, AMZN, GOOGL: Capex dollars could slip between quarters (we think low-single-digit percent of 2027 capex at risk of moving right) even if full-year budgets hold. We would watch for any change in 2027 capex tone on the Oct 27-29 calls.
- NVDA: A one- to two-quarter slip in shell and power readiness could shift timing of rack deliveries into 2027, particularly for liquid-cooled Rubin-class deployments. We do not see order risk, but possibly some timing noise.
- AAPL: Limited. Apple's U.S. server buildout for Private Cloud Compute is small versus hyperscalers, and HVC does not cite it.

What would change our view: A second contractor or an owner confirming schedule slips, or any hyperscaler flagging "capacity availability" as a constraint on guidance.

subject: AAPL: App developers in Brazil report new Apple payment-terms notices ahead of CADE deadline (12 devs, early)
body:
Calder Row Research | Mobile Ecosystem Checks | Oct 13

AAPL: Brazil App Store terms - early developer chatter

Summary: Over the past week we spoke with 12 iOS developers with meaningful Brazilian user bases (4 games, 3 subscription media, 3 fintech/marketplace, 2 utilities). Seven told us they received an email or developer-portal notice from Apple in the past 10 days about "updated terms for alternative payment processing and external purchase links in Brazil." Five had not received anything.

Background: Brazil's antitrust authority has an open case on iOS payment and steering restrictions. Public reporting says a compliance deadline is under discussion, and we have not found a public ruling that sets terms. Apple has appealed parts of the process in the past.

What the developers told us (unverified, anecdotal):
- Five of the seven said the notice referenced a reduced commission on externally processed purchases and a separate "core technology" style fee. None could cite the percentages from memory. Two said the numbers were in a document they had not yet opened.
- Three said the language was "conditional on regulatory timing." One described the notice as a draft that "might not go live."
- No developer had yet seen a change in how the checkout flow works in production.

Why it matters: Brazil is a small share of Apple's Services revenue (we estimate low-single-digit percent of App Store billings). The larger question is whether a Brazilian outcome sets a template, and whether Apple is pre-positioning terms globally before similar proceedings elsewhere. At the moment we cannot separate a real rollout plan from a contingency.

What we are watching:
1. Any filing or public order from the authority setting a compliance date
2. Whether developers see the terms move into a live portal
3. Whether Apple comments on it during the Oct 29 call

Our take: Monitor only. No change to Services estimates; the sample is small and nothing is confirmed. We will re-poll in two weeks and can share notes with the 12 developers on request.

Tomás Reyes | Calder Row Research
reason: Early, anecdotal developer reports of new Apple payment terms ahead of a pending Brazilian antitrust process. The legal outcome and fee terms are unconfirmed and the revenue exposure looks small, so this is a signal to monitor rather than act on.
angle: developing regulatory or legal process

FDA approves Lumenor Pharma's once-weekly treatment for moderate-to-severe psoriasis

DOCKET WIRE | BREAKING | Oct 13, 2026 10:42am ET

Supreme Court agrees to hear tribal water-rights case with seven-state implications

WASHINGTON - The U.S. Supreme Court on Tuesday granted certiorari in a long-running dispute over whether federal treaty obligations require the Interior Department to secure water deliveries for several tribal nations in the lower Colorado River basin. Argument is expected in the February sitting, with a decision by the end of June.

Key points:
- The Ninth Circuit held last year that the government has an affirmative duty to assess tribal water needs before approving new interstate allocation guidelines. Three states petitioned for review, arguing the ruling would freeze allocation planning.
- The Solicitor General's office supported review but took no position on the merits.
- Two amicus briefs from agricultural water districts and a coalition of municipal utilities argue that a broad reading of the duty could delay the post-2026 operating guidelines by years.
- Three justices requested supplemental briefing on whether the case is moot if the Interior Department finalizes its new guidelines before argument.

What to watch: Briefing deadlines run through January. Interior has said it expects to publish final operating guidelines in the first quarter, which could narrow the questions before the Court.

Background and the full order list are available in the Docket Wire Court Tracker. Attorneys for the petitioners declined to comment. Counsel for the tribal respondents said they were "pleased the Court will address the government's trust obligations."

sender: Gideon Falk, Macro & Technology Strategist, Ashbury Cross Securities
subject: AM Strategy: GPU-backed credit spreads widen 60bp as 10-yr hits 4.9% - what it means for NVDA's non-hyperscaler demand into FQ3
body:
ASHBURY CROSS SECURITIES | Morning Strategy | Tuesday Oct 13

Markets: Equity futures are flat. The 10-year Treasury yield is at 4.89% (+6bp on the day, +31bp over the past month) after yesterday's firm Treasury auction. The dollar is little changed.

Key item: financing costs for AI infrastructure outside the hyperscalers

Over the past three weeks, the spread on GPU-collateralized ABS and delayed-draw term loans issued by independent GPU-cloud operators has widened by about 60bp to roughly SOFR+485 on the most recent print, per our credit desk's tracking of eight deals. Two planned issues were pulled last week, and a third was repriced 75bp wider with a tighter advance rate (down to 72% from 80% of GPU purchase price).

Why it matters for Nvidia: We estimate non-hyperscaler buyers (neoclouds, sovereign programs and enterprise) at about 24% of Nvidia data center revenue this fiscal year, of which independent GPU clouds are roughly 11-13 points. Those buyers fund a large share of purchases with asset-backed debt, which is much more rate-sensitive than the hyperscalers' operating cash flow. Higher spreads and lower advance rates raise the equity check required per rack, which in our view could delay or shrink some orders booked for FQ4 and FQ1.

Our read: This does not affect FQ3 shipments, which are already financed. The risk is to the order trajectory that supports the FQ4/FQ1 guide. If financing stays at these levels through November, we would expect management to be more cautious about the non-hyperscaler mix. We estimate every 10% reduction in neocloud orders is worth about $0.7bn of quarterly revenue.

For those with NVDA positioning built mainly around the hyperscaler capex story, this is a smaller factor. For books exposed to the neocloud/sovereign upside, the financing trend is worth monitoring closely ahead of the November report.

No change to our NVDA rating or estimates today.

Gideon Falk | Ashbury Cross Securities

subject: Macro Strategy: India trade-talk chatter on a revived digital levy - early, unconfirmed, tails for platform names
body:
Pelham Cross Securities | Global Macro Strategy | Oct 13

India: trade talks, the rupee and a possible digital levy - an early signal to watch

Background. The rupee is within 1% of its record low, and the U.S.-India trade negotiations face a self-imposed late-October target. Local business press has run two pieces in the past 72 hours, citing unnamed finance ministry officials, saying New Delhi is weighing a revival of the 6% equalisation levy on foreign digital advertising and a new charge on app-store billings. The idea is reportedly being floated as a bargaining chip and as a revenue offset if tariff concessions are made.

What we know and don't know:
- There is no draft notification, and neither ministry has commented on the record.
- A second source we speak to regularly, a former trade official, said the app-store charge is "being discussed, not designed."
- We have not been able to confirm whether the levy would apply to advertising revenue booked outside India.

Why it matters beyond India. If implemented, we see two read-throughs: (1) Alphabet's advertising and Apple's App Store/services billings would both be directly exposed; (2) other large markets may cite India as a precedent in their own digital tax discussions.

Sizing. Our rough estimate is that India accounts for around 2-3% of Apple revenue, including a fast-growing iPhone base, and 1-2% of Alphabet revenue. A 6% levy absorbed by the companies is therefore a small direct hit, but the signal matters more than the number. We would also watch whether any levy is paired with a rupee-linked pricing response on iPhones and Play-billed apps.

What we would watch: a formal draft, a statement from the commerce ministry before the late-October deadline, and any hint of a similar discussion in Indonesia or Brazil.

Positioning: no change to our macro views. We flag this as a monitor item for platform and services exposure.

Dominic Ashworth | Pelham Cross Securities
Analyst certification and disclosures at pelhamcross.com/disclosures

DOCKETLINE | TECH ENFORCEMENT MONITOR | Issue 41 | Oct 13

HEADLINE ITEM: Information-gathering stage on AI-assistant bundling

Our document-capture panel (9 corporate customers and 3 reseller partners across the EU) shows that an EU member-state competition authority has sent questionnaires to enterprise buyers of cloud productivity suites. The questions concern how AI assistants are priced, bundled and defaulted within office suites.

What the questionnaires ask (7 documents reviewed):
- Whether customers could buy the productivity suite without the AI assistant, and at what price difference
- Whether switching assistants requires changing suites
- Whether pricing changed on renewal after the AI assistant was introduced
- Interoperability of third-party assistants with the suite

Companies named in the documents:
Microsoft (M365 / Copilot): 5 of 7
Google (Workspace / Gemini): 5 of 7
Other vendors: 2 of 7

Process status (our reading):
- Stage: preliminary market inquiry. This is NOT a formal proceeding and no statement of objections has been issued.
- Response deadline cited in the questionnaires: Nov 6
- The authority has not commented publicly. We could not confirm whether other member states are coordinating.
- Past inquiries that began with customer questionnaires (cloud licensing, 2024) took about 14 months to reach any formal step, and about 40% of them closed without one.

Our view: Watch for (1) a public announcement from the authority, (2) similar questionnaires in a second member state, and (3) any disclosure in the companies' upcoming 10-Qs. We put the probability of a formal case within 6 months at roughly 25-30%. This is a low-confidence estimate.

Other items this week (summaries only): Korea app-store fee order (no change), Brazil digital markets bill (committee stage).

STATEHOUSE & COURTS WEEKLY | Regulatory & Court Watch | Tuesday, Oct 13

Top items for compliance and government-affairs readers.

ENERGY - FERC cost-allocation order (Midwest transmission)
The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission issued an order on rehearing that upholds a regional cost-allocation formula for a 345kV transmission line spanning three states. Two state utility commissions had argued the formula over-assigned costs to their ratepayers. The order is not final until the 60-day appeal window closes. Practitioners expect at least one petition for review in the D.C. Circuit.

COURTS - Mineral royalty ruling
The Texas Supreme Court held 6-3 that post-production deduction language in a 1990s-era lease did not allow the operator to net gathering costs against royalty payments. The decision applies to a narrow set of leases with similar wording. Plaintiffs' counsel estimate affected royalty owners number in the low thousands.

AVIATION - FAA airworthiness directive
The FAA issued an emergency directive requiring repetitive propeller blade inspections on a regional turboprop model after two reported cracking incidents. Operators must complete the first inspection within 30 flight-hours. Roughly 140 aircraft are on the U.S. registry.

FOOD & BEVERAGE - State liquor distribution law
A state law taking effect Jan 1 narrows exclusive-distributor franchise protections for craft brewers producing under 15,000 barrels a year. Distributors' trade association said it is considering a constitutional challenge.

HEALTH - FDA warning letters

COVERLINE WIRE | MEDIA & ADVERTISING | Oct 13, 9:14am ET

UNCONFIRMED: Large packaged-goods advertiser reportedly moving Q4 search dollars toward Amazon ads

A global household-products advertiser, one of the five biggest CPG ad spenders in the U.S., has instructed its media agencies to reallocate roughly $150 million of Q4 paid-search budget from Google Search to Amazon Sponsored Products and Sponsored Brands, according to two people at agencies on the account and a third person briefed on the planning. Coverline has not seen the written brief.

Details from the sources:
- The shift would cover brand and non-brand keywords for the advertiser's home-care and personal-care lines, with the change taking effect Oct 26.
- One agency source said the move follows an internal test in which the advertiser saw about 20% lower cost per incremental sale on Amazon during the Prime Big Deal Days window than on Google Shopping campaigns.
- A second source said part of the motive is anxiety about reduced click-through on commercial queries since the roll-out of expanded AI answers in search, but said the client's own data on this was "inconclusive."
- The third person said the reallocation is "not final" and could be scaled to $75-100 million if the Amazon results soften in the first two weeks.

Context: The advertiser's total U.S. paid-search spend is estimated at $1.2 billion a year, which makes $150 million about 12% of that. The company's total ad spend is dispersed across TV, social, retail media and search.

Responses: The advertiser declined to comment. Google and Amazon did not respond to requests for comment by publication time.

Coverline's view: A single advertiser's reallocation is not a trend, and similar test-and-shift stories have fizzled before. If other large advertisers describe similar moves, it would be worth watching for the Oct 27 and Oct 29 prints.

We will update this alert if we can confirm the details.

subject: Heard something from a couple of DSP owners - peak route allotments
body:
Raj,

Hope the quarter's treating you well. Flagging something from my usual circle that I can't fully back up yet, so treat it as a rumor.

Over the past week, two Amazon delivery service partner owners I talk to regularly (one in the Southeast, one in the Mid-Atlantic, both with 40-plus vans) independently said their Amazon station managers have told them to plan for fewer peak-season routes than last year. The numbers they gave were roughly 8-12% below last year's Nov-Dec allotments, versus the normal pattern of a 5-10% increase. Both also mentioned the stations are being asked to "pilot" a new per-package pay element in addition to the standard route-based rate, and that it was to be rolled out to a small set of stations first.

A choice screen on the installed base would be more consequential than a new-device-only version. The EU experience suggests share leakage from choice screens is modest, but we would not extrapolate from one region to another without seeing the final design.

What is NOT known: the final text, the compliance date (contacts range from mid-2027 to 'next fiscal year'), whether the draft is binding or advisory, and whether Apple's iOS defaults fall under the same process (contacts say it is Android-focused for now).

We have not changed estimates. We would watch for (1) the final guidance after the comment window, (2) any Google public filing, and (3) whether Korea or India regulators cite the Japan design.

body:
Hallmark Row Global Research | Global Macro Weekly | Oct 13, 2026

China's deflation grind: producer prices still negative, consumer inflation near zero

Summary: September data released over the weekend showed China's PPI at -2.3% y/y (vs. -2.5% in August) and CPI at +0.1% y/y. We think headline improvement masks weak underlying demand and flag three implications for emerging market policy.

1. Domestic demand: Core CPI excluding food and energy is running at +0.4% y/y. Property-related components remain negative, and services inflation continues to drift lower. We expect the PBoC to cut the seven-day reverse repo by 10bp in Q4, with a 50bp RRR cut as an alternative.

2. Export prices: Our estimate of Chinese manufacturers' export price index is down 3.1% y/y, contributing to disinflation pressures in Southeast Asia, Mexico and Eastern Europe. Where currencies are weak relative to the renminbi, this effect is partly offset.

3. EM central banks: We expect Bank of Thailand and Bank Negara Malaysia to remain on hold through Q1, while Chile, Poland and Hungary have room to cut an additional 25-50bp each. Brazil and Indonesia are constrained by currency considerations.

Market view: Overweight local-currency bonds in Poland and Mexico; neutral on China government bonds; underweight CNH vs. USD on a three-month view with target 7.32.

Risks: A larger-than-expected fiscal package at the November NPC Standing Committee would lift commodity demand and ease deflation pressures faster than our base case.

Data tables and charts are attached. Next week: Eurozone flash PMIs and the Swedish Riksbank.

Annika Brandt, PhD
Chief Economist, Hallmark Row Global Research

sender: Hannah Okonkwo-Reyes, Senior Semiconductor Analyst, Pembrook Rowe & Co.
subject: NVDA: HBM step-ups + rack-level mix pressure FQ3/FQ4 gross margin - we are 140-200bp below Street; EPS est. trimmed
body:
PEMBROOK ROWE & CO. | Semiconductors | Company Update

NVIDIA (NVDA) - Buy | Price target $235 (from $240)
Margin debate heats up: our supply-chain work points to GM below the Street path

Bottom line: We keep our Buy rating but trim FQ3/FQ4 EPS on gross margin. We now see two cost drivers the Street is not capturing, one in memory and one in product mix.

1. HBM pricing. Our checks with three memory-module and substrate suppliers indicate that HBM3E 12-high and early HBM4 contracts for calendar 2027 have been reset ~12-15% above first-half pricing. We estimate HBM is now ~21-23% of Blackwell Ultra BOM. Nvidia has long-term agreements, but the new tranche applies to volume added after August.

2. Rack-level mix. A rising share of shipments is full GB300 NVL72 racks, in which Nvidia includes more third-party content (compute trays, copper cabling, and liquid cooling). Revenue per rack rises, but the gross margin percentage on that incremental revenue is lower. We estimate racks are ~58% of FQ3 data center revenue vs. ~49% in FQ2.

3. Offsets. Higher networking attach and software in the full-stack deals offset part of the pressure. We do not model any price cut on Blackwell.

Estimate changes (non-GAAP):
| | FQ3E new | FQ3E old | Cons. | FQ4E new | FQ4E old | Cons. |
| Revenue ($bn) | 77.0 | 77.0 | 76.0 | 84.5 | 84.5 | 83.0 |
| Gross margin | 72.0% | 73.2% | 73.4% | 71.0% | 72.8% | 73.0% |
| EPS | $1.31 | $1.34 | $1.33 | $1.46 | $1.51 | $1.50 |

Why it matters for positioning: Revenue is tracking at or above the Street, so we think the stock debate has shifted to margin sustainability. Investors who are long on the thesis that gross margins hold at ~73% through 2027 should be most concerned about this. For holders who care mainly about unit volumes and revenue growth, this is a smaller issue. We see FQ3 GM as the first test; management has previously guided to "mid-70s" on a full-year basis.

Risks to our view: Management could pass through higher costs, shift mix toward higher-margin networking, or buy HBM at better terms. We would revisit if the FQ3 call points to tighter pricing discipline.

Hannah Okonkwo-Reyes | Pembrook Rowe & Co. Equity Research
Analyst certification and important disclosures at the end of this report.
reason: Differentiated supply-chain work suggests NVDA gross margin could be 140-200bp below consensus for FQ3 and FQ4 because of HBM price resets and rack-level mix, a specific and testable challenge to the margin-hold view. Its importance depends on whether the desk's NVDA position leans on margin expansion versus volume, which the note itself says.

TECH ENFORCEMENT MONITOR | Government Affairs | Oct 13

What happened: The Commerce Department's export control bureau published a notice extending the public comment period by 30 days, to Nov 16, on a proposed rule that would change how licenses are reviewed for advanced AI accelerators shipped to third-country data centers. The extension followed requests from industry associations.

What the proposal would do (per the Federal Register notice):
- Move from product-threshold-based approvals to a customer-and-site-based review for large clusters (the draft cites deployments above a set aggregate compute level).
- Require end-user certifications and periodic site audits for destinations in a defined list of transshipment-risk countries.
- Create a presumption of denial for clusters where the ultimate parent is headquartered in a restricted jurisdiction.

Docket activity: Of the 212 comments filed so far, Nvidia filed a 19-page submission arguing the site-audit requirement is "operationally unworkable" for cloud-delivered capacity and that the aggregate-compute trigger would capture routine enterprise deployments. Two other chip firms and three cloud providers filed shorter letters. Several think tanks support the stricter approach.

What we do not know: The bureau has not said whether a final rule would be effective on publication or phased in. A senior official told reporters last week that the agency is "not committed" to the current text.

Timeline: Comment period closes Nov 16. A final rule is unlikely before Q1 2027 on typical timelines, though the agency has moved faster on earlier AI-related actions.

Why it matters: Sovereign and Middle East/Southeast Asia buildouts are a growing share of Nvidia's data center demand. Any final rule that adds approval friction could delay shipments, but the outcome is open and the text may change.

Northvale Field Research | Consumer Hardware | Channel Check - EARLY / LOW CONFIDENCE

Team,

Sharing an early observation from our weekly delivery-window scrape and a small round of retailer calls. We want to be clear up front that the sample is thin and we have not yet been able to confirm the cause.

What we are seeing:
- Apple online store estimated delivery for iPhone 18 Pro Max (256GB, most popular colors) has shortened to 5-8 days in the U.S., Japan and the U.K. as of this morning, from 3-4 weeks at the start of October. The base iPhone 18 and the Pro are showing 1-3 days in all three markets.
- Over the same period, three large premium Android flagships have gone to bundled promotions: one major Korean OEM offers a free tablet or trade-in uplift of up to $250 in the U.S. and U.K., and another brand cut its flagship price by 12% in Germany.
- Retailer calls (9 stores, 4 national chains/carriers, 3 independent resellers): 5 said Pro Max inventory is 'easy to get' now, 3 said 'no change', and 1 said allocation remains tight for the 1TB model. Two staff mentioned weaker foot traffic than last year's launch window, but anecdotes vary.

How to read it (cautiously):
- Could be a sign of softer Pro Max demand, particularly if it matches the December-quarter build chatter some of you have heard.
- Could just be supply catching up after a constrained launch, with mix shifting between configurations.
- Could reflect Apple managing online stock differently from store allocation. We have seen delivery windows compress for operational reasons in past cycles.

What would increase our confidence: delivery windows staying short for another 7-10 days, carriers confirming their promo spend, and any move in supplier order commentary. We plan to re-run the scrape on Thursday and Monday and add Canada and Australia.

Not in our numbers: we have made no change to our iPhone unit estimates and we are not suggesting a call on the December quarter off this alone.

Happy to share the raw scrape file if useful.

Kenji Arvidsson
Northvale Field Research

DANUBIA CAPITAL MARKETS | CEE Strategy | Oct 13

Poland: NBP likely to deliver 25bp in November, but guidance is turning more cautious

September CPI came in at 3.4% y/y (consensus 3.5%), with core at 3.3%. Services inflation remains the sticky component at 5.1% y/y, driven by rents and insurance. Wage growth in the enterprise sector slowed to 7.2% y/y from 7.6%, which is helpful but still above the level consistent with 2.5% inflation.

Our view:
- We expect a 25bp cut at the November 4-5 meeting, taking the reference rate to 4.75%. The MPC's language has shifted from "gradual normalization" to "data-dependent," and two members dissented in September in favor of a pause.
- Fiscal risk is the swing factor. The 2027 draft budget implies a general government deficit near 6.1% of GDP, versus the 5.5% the Ministry of Finance signaled in spring. Our debt-supply model points to roughly PLN 40bn of extra net issuance next year.
- Curve: We like 2s10s steepeners at current levels. The 10-year POLGB at 5.6% already prices in some of the fiscal slippage, but not a downgrade outlook revision.
- FX: EUR/PLN has traded a narrow 4.24-4.31 range for six weeks. Carry-to-vol is still attractive vs. HUF, but a dovish surprise could take EUR/PLN toward 4.35.

Risks: a sharper-than-expected NBP cut, a negative rating action in the 4Q review cycle, and energy price pass-through into regulated tariffs from January.

Trade recommendations (indicative): Receive 2y PLN swaps vs. pay 10y; hold long PLN vs. EUR with stops at 4.18.

Katarzyna Wrobel | Danubia Capital Markets

subject: ALERT: Blackwell spot rental quotes reportedly firming at secondary GPU brokers - two sources, unconfirmed
body:
COMPUTE WIRE | Alert | Oct 13, 9:42am ET

Spot rental quotes for Nvidia Blackwell-class instances are said to be firming at secondary GPU brokers, according to two brokerage contacts spoken to by Compute Wire.

What we heard:
- One New Jersey-based broker, which places short-term capacity for startups and research labs, said quotes for 8-GPU Blackwell nodes on one-to-three-month terms rose about 9-11% over the past two weeks, after having drifted lower since June. The broker described availability as "noticeably tighter" since late September.
- A second broker, based in Singapore, said it had seen "a few" inbound requests it could not fill from AI labs that had previously sourced from large cloud providers on-demand. It did not quantify the change in quotes.
- A third broker told us its quotes were unchanged and that it saw nothing unusual.

Context and caveats:
- Neither broker has visibility into hyperscaler-level supply, and secondary markets are a small share of overall GPU consumption.
- Spot prices can move on a handful of large orders, and there is no public index that covers these quotes. Compute Wire's own tracker is not live for Blackwell instances.
- Quotes are indicative, not transacted. We have not verified figures with any marketplace operator.
- Seasonal training-run schedules before year-end could explain some of the move.

Nvidia did not respond to a request for comment. We will update this alert if further data points emerge.

Compute Wire provides market information for informational purposes only and does not guarantee accuracy.
reason: Early, anecdotal broker commentary suggests Blackwell rental pricing is firming, which could signal tighter near-term GPU supply for Nvidia. Only two sources, no transacted data, one dissenting broker and an unclear read to hyperscale demand, so it needs confirmation before it can matter.
angle: anecdotal channel datapoint needing confirmation

sender: Ingrid Solheim, Nordic Macro Strategist, Fjellstrand Capital Research
subject: Nordic Macro Letter (Oct 13): Riksbank pause, Norges Bank's December dilemma, and the krona's carry problem
body:
FJELLSTRAND CAPITAL RESEARCH | NORDIC MACRO LETTER | Oct 13, 2026

Headline view: Both Nordic central banks are done cutting for now, but for different reasons. Sweden is pausing because inflation is back near target. Norway is pausing because it has little room to move.

1) Sweden: Riksbank on hold at 1.75% through year-end
- Sept CPIF printed 2.0% y/y (consensus 2.1%), with core CPIF at 2.3%. Food inflation eased to 3.1% from 4.4% in June.
- Housing activity is recovering. Existing-home prices are +3.2% y/y in the three largest metros. The Riksbank has said repeatedly that it does not want to stoke a new leverage cycle.
- Wage settlements for 2026-27 are tracking 3.4%, in line with the "norm" set by the export sector. We see no wage-driven reason to cut again.
- Call: hold at the Nov 19 meeting, with the first move in H2 2027 and the next move more likely a hike than a cut.

2) Norway: Norges Bank's December dilemma
- Underlying inflation (CPI-ATE) is 3.0% y/y, still above the 2% target, while mainland GDP growth has slowed to roughly 0.9% annualized in Q3.
- The policy rate is 4.0%. The bank's own path implies one cut by March, but the krone is weaker than its forecast assumed. A weaker krone raises imported inflation and argues for patience.
- We expect no change in November. The December Monetary Policy Report is the real risk event: a revised path with fewer cuts would likely push the krone higher.

3) Krona carry: crowded, but not for much longer
- SEK/NOK has been range-bound for eight weeks. Positioning data show real-money long-NOK positions at a 15-month high.
- With a Brent-linked terms-of-trade tailwind fading and Norway's fiscal impulse turning neutral in 2027, we see risk-reward skewed toward a modest NOK pullback versus EUR into year-end.

Charts and tables attached (policy rate paths, wage settlements, housing indicators).

Trade ideas: Receive 2y SEK swaps vs. pay 2y NOK swaps (target 35bp, stop 15bp); long EUR/NOK at 11.85, target 12.20.

Ingrid Solheim | Fjellstrand Capital Research
This material is for institutional clients only.

INDIA: SEPTEMBER CPI 3.9% Y/Y (CONSENSUS 4.1%; AUGUST 3.6%)

- Headline CPI rose to 3.9% y/y from 3.6% in August, below the 4.1% consensus in a Reuters-style poll of economists.

- 10-year G-sec yield rose 4bp to 6.31%. The rupee was little changed at 87.9 per dollar.

Watch next
- Oct 28: RBI Monetary Policy Committee minutes
- Nov 12: October CPI

body:
WEXCOMBE POLICY RESEARCH | Tax Alert | Oct 13, 2026

Treasury and the IRS published final regulations this morning implementing the 100% expensing and domestic R&D expensing provisions enacted last year. The final text tracks the June proposed rules closely. The changes are cosmetic: a tighter definition of "qualified production property," a safe harbor for software development cost allocation, and a transition election for taxpayers that amortized 2022-2024 domestic R&D.

What the final rules do for large technology filers
- Confirm that servers, networking gear and purpose-built data center equipment placed in service in the U.S. qualify for immediate expensing.
- Leave structural shells and land on 39-year schedules, as the proposal did.
- Allow an election to accelerate remaining unamortized 2022-2024 domestic R&D over one or two years, as most filers already assumed.

Our estimate of the 2026 cash-tax deferral versus the pre-law regime (all five names are covered in our megacap tax tracker)
- Amazon: ~$9-10bn, driven by fulfillment and AWS equipment
- Microsoft: ~$7-8bn
- Alphabet: ~$6-7bn
- Apple: ~$2bn (the R&D election is the main driver)

One of Amazon's larger AI-model investees closed a priced equity round in mid-September at a valuation well above the prior mark. Amazon holds part of its position as convertible notes carried at fair value, with changes run through other income. Based on the disclosed note amount and the implied step-up, we model a pre-tax non-operating gain of about $7.4bn in 3Q, which is roughly $0.54 per share after tax.

A reported GAAP EPS "beat" of this size would therefore reflect the investment mark, not the operating business. Operating income, AWS growth and the 4Q guide are what should drive the stock. The gain also complicates any quick headline comparison of EPS to consensus, and Amazon may well call out the item in the release.

No change to our rating or price target. Full model and a revised other-income schedule are attached.

sender: Graham Pellerin, Principal, Pellerin Trade & Policy Advisors
subject: Section 232 electronics inquiry - heard downstream tariff language is being drafted (post-midterm timing?)
body:
Ellen,

Sharing something from a few hallway conversations in D.C. last week. None of this is official, so treat it accordingly.

Background: Commerce's Section 232 investigation on semiconductors and "derivative products" has been open for months. The public docket has focused on chips themselves, and the products that contain them have been treated as a follow-on question.

What I'm hearing from two people close to the process (a former colleague at Commerce and outside counsel representing an importers' group):

1. Staff are drafting language that would extend a tariff to downstream electronics, including servers and networking gear, smartphones and consumer devices, using the chip content of the product as the basis. Counsel described a tiered approach with percentage rates pegged to chip value.

2. There is serious discussion of an offset or exemption credit for companies with documented U.S. manufacturing or data center investment commitments. Who qualifies and how it is measured is unresolved, and that detail will matter far more than the headline rate.

3. Timing: both sources believe a determination would not be released before the Nov 3 midterms and could slip into December. One said the White House wants it as leverage in ongoing trade talks. Another said the statutory clock gives them room.

Why it touches your names. If the framework holds: Apple (device imports, with the offset question tied to its U.S. investment pledges), Nvidia (chips and systems assembled abroad, with a possible exemption for U.S.-bound product built under U.S. commitments), Amazon (devices plus the AWS server import bill), and Microsoft and Alphabet (server and networking hardware for data centers, a capex cost issue). Each would be affected differently, and I can't tell you who would come out ahead.

I would put the odds that it reaches the final stage in this form at no better than even. The industry is lobbying hard, and a draft is a long way from a proclamation.

Happy to jump on a call, but I'd rather not put more in writing. I'll let you know if I hear anything firmer.

Graham

Graham Pellerin | Pellerin Trade & Policy Advisors
Washington, D.C.
reason: A policy contact relays unconfirmed reports that a Section 232 process could extend tariffs to downstream electronics, with an unresolved offset for U.S. investment, which would affect all five targets in different ways. The process is ongoing, timing is after the midterms, and the source puts odds at no better than even. That is a credible developing regulatory signal to monitor, not a confirmed change.

Raj,

Good catching up last week. Two things from client conversations over the past ten days that struck me as different in tone from what I was hearing in the summer. They're probably unrelated, but you asked me to flag anything about enterprise IT budgets.

1) Apple / Mac. A 22,000-seat financial services client had planned to move to a Mac-heavy fleet at the next refresh, which they'd been calling a 2027 project. 2) Microsoft / EA renewals. Three clients with EAs up for renewal between January and March said Microsoft account teams are more flexible than at any point since 2022 on Copilot bundling. One was offered Copilot at roughly a 20% discount to list if they commit to a larger E5 footprint. The tone from Microsoft reps went from 'Copilot is a separate SKU' to 'let's package it'. Two of the three said they plan to adopt Copilot for a subset of users only.

My read is that both vendors are working harder for enterprise budget in a tighter-IT-spend environment. That's a tone shift, not a data point. I wouldn't base a position on five conversations, but I did want you to know.

Happy to ask more clients if it would be useful.

Teresa
